thesis: Huntington Ingalls is the only builder of US nuclear submarines and aircraft carriers, it has a record $57.3bn backlog worth 4.2 years of revenue, and in its Q2 FY2026 release it beat by 37%, lifted segment margin to 6.6% from 5.6%, raised FY26 shipbuilding revenue guidance to $10.2-10.4bn and raised the low end of its margin guidance — and the stock is down 32% from its high, 3% above a 120-day low, at ~14.6x annualised H1 EPS against GD at 19.5x, LMT 16.9x and NOC 16.6x. The de-rating that hit the primes is a bet on US defense budget growth slowing after FY2027; applying it to the one franchise with a 20-year, single-source order book and no competitor is the mispricing.
key_risk: Free cash flow was negative $150M in Q2 against positive $730M a year earlier. HII is a capital-intensive shipbuilder ramping two submarine classes at once, and if the working-capital drain is structural rather than timing, the reaffirmed $500-600M FY26 free cash flow is missed and a 14.6x multiple is not cheap for a business that cannot fund its own ramp. The second risk is execution: Q1 margin fell to 5.6% on pre-COVID-era fixed-price contracts, and that is the same class of problem now costing Northrop ~$2.0bn on B-21.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that a shipbuilding monopoly is a monopsony customer in disguise: HII has exactly one buyer, the Navy sets the price, and margin has sat at 5-7% for years against 10%+ at the primes, so a persistent discount to GD and LMT is the correct price for a business with no pricing power rather than an error. The answer is that the discount is not being argued away, it is being sized — the target is 16.5x, still below GD today, on earnings carried by a backlog that is already contracted rather than forecast. The thesis does not need HII to earn prime-like margins; it needs 6.5-8% on roughly 40% more revenue.

thesis: The fear that de-rated managed care is the medical cost ratio, and UnitedHealth has guided it down twice: the FY2026 MCR outlook went from 88.8% plus or minus 50bp in January to 88.1% plus or minus 25bp in the Q2 release, with adjusted EPS guided to $19.50-20.00 and operating cash flow to about $24bn. Q2 delivered an 86.7% MCR, $6.38 adjusted EPS and $11.1bn of operating cash flow at 1.9 times net income, and the company is deliberately shedding Medicare Advantage membership — down 965,000 since year-end — to hold MA margins above 3%. Thirty-four analysts cover it with zero sell ratings, the last two quarters beat by 28.8% and 8.9%, and the stock is 17.8% off its high having based between 362.60 and 387.52 for two weeks. The trade is to let Tuesday morning resolve it and buy the confirmation.
key_risk: The quality of the Q2 beat is the weak point: the 86.7% MCR was helped by $860M of net favorable prior period development, roughly $0.57 a share after tax or about 9% of adjusted EPS, so reserve releases are flattering the cost-trend story the whole thesis rests on. If Q3 shows cost trend without that cushion, the MCR guide goes the other way and a 19.2x multiple is not cheap. Second, the release reports membership contracting 965,000 while its own people-served table shows the Medicare Advantage line down 880,000, and does not reconcile them — a disclosure the Q3 report needs to clear up. Third, waiting means forgoing the entire gap if the print is good, which is the explicit price of this structure.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that 19.2x forward earnings and 14x operating cash flow is not a de-rated price for a business losing a million Medicare Advantage members a year and guiding H2 adjusted EPS of $5.89-6.39 against $13.61 in H1 — the stock may simply be repricing to slower growth, in which case the 437 high is not a level to recover but one to forget. The answer is that the H2 step-down is Medicare seasonality rather than deterioration, with an implied Q4 near $2.0 against an actual $2.11 in Q4 2025, and that the membership loss is a chosen trade of volume for margin stated as such. The honest concession is that this is a de-rating-reversal idea and not a value idea, and it is written that way rather than dressed up as cheap.

thesis: Direction is recorded as `buy` because this amends the live LONG position of that name; the recommended action is to CLOSE it. Delta reported Q3 on 2026-10-09 and cut FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance from $6.50-7.50 to $5.10-5.60 while absorbing a $6bn fuel increase, with Q3 fuel up 62% year on year and $500M worse than the July guide. Worse, the Q4 guide assumes all-in fuel of about $4.25/gal struck against the forward curve as of 2026-10-02, and Brent has gone from $101.49 on 10-07 to roughly $105 after the Riyadh strikes — the central cost assumption is already behind. The entry is fixed at 83.00, so the 94.50 target needs +15% from a business whose earnings power was just cut 25%. The catalyst has been delivered and refused; the position is retired rather than re-targeted.
key_risk: Closing here sells a stock that absorbed the bad news well: DAL traded down to 79.16 on the print and still closed 82.17, +0.04%, on the heaviest volume of the month at 11.93M. Delta is the only US airline that owns a refinery, worth about $0.40/gal of its own $4.25 Q4 assumption, so it is the name that re-rates fastest on any crude reversal — and this exit forgoes that. The residual risk of the exit itself is that the discretionary close is not taken, in which case the unchanged 78.10 stop governs, 4.9% below Friday.
counter_argument: The strongest case for holding is that the quarter was a revenue beat with premium demand up 16% and Q4 revenue guided up about 20%, so the entire miss was a fuel pass-through — cyclical, not a franchise problem. That case is sound about the business and still loses on the arithmetic: it is an argument for owning Delta at some price, not an argument that 94.50 is reachable from a fixed 83.00 entry while the fuel curve is still rising and the airline itself has told you its assumption was struck eleven days ago.

evidence.detail: Read the 2026-10-09 8-K and the same-day 10-Q for the quarter ended 2026-09-30: FY26 adjusted EPS guided to $5.10-5.60 from $6.50-7.50, pre-tax ~$4.5bn, FCF ~$2.5bn from $3-4bn, Q4 all-in fuel ~$4.25/gal against the 2026-10-02 forward curve including ~$0.40/gal refinery benefit, non-fuel unit costs +7.3%
